content:
Earlier this year when Apple launched the MacBook Neo, the personal computer market was completely caught off guard. Although the laptop's aggressive pricing strategy has since been forced to adjust in response to market conditions, it has taken several months before we have seen Windows-based competitors successively announce their own competing products. HP's turn has come today — the company has unveiled a new laptop equipped with an OLED display, also starting at US$699, but with quite a few strings attached.

Top comment by TurboFool

Recently there has been a flood of Windows news that has absolutely nothing to do with Google, and that is worrying. Some of the content only has the most tenuous connection to Google — at best it is an ARM device, or could perhaps be stretched to be called the same category of product as an Android device, but that is already a very strained argument. Yet this is an x86-architecture Windows laptop — there is simply no justification for including it in this discussion. I migrated here from sites like AP and AA, and watched those platforms gradually fill up with off-topic content to pad post counts, which greatly concerns me. I really do not want to lose another one.

The overall design of the HP OmniBook 5 14 looks like a budget, colour-bodied version of the MacBook Neo, resembling a blend of the more refined and understated green and blue shades of the iPad Air lineup. At just 11.77mm thick and with a 14-inch screen yet weighing only 2.56 pounds, it would have been a perfect choice for the back-to-school shopping season — but HP appears to have missed the ideal timing. That said, the 14-inch screen is the laptop's biggest highlight: rather than the IPS panels commonly found in products at this price point, it uses one of two OLED displays, which we will go into in more detail shortly. The sides of the chassis come with two full-function USB-C ports and a headphone jack, and when you open the lid, a full-HD camera supporting Windows Hello greets you.

On the hardware specifications, HP says it supports up to an Intel Core 7 processor, though the model currently on show is the only option available. Battery life on paper is quite impressive — up to 42 hours of local video playback — but the battery capacity has not been disclosed. That said, it must be acknowledged that local video playback tests may not fully reflect real-world usage. HP says the device is compatible with the company's 65W mini GaN charger, which I presume will be included in the box. Beyond that, dual microphones and a Poly Studio-tuned audio system are all the specifications known so far. If you feel there is still a great deal of information that has not been revealed, you are not alone.

Firstly, it remains unclear which processor the US$700 version of the laptop will use, making it difficult to compare with Apple's A18 Pro. HP has also chosen not to disclose any storage or memory configurations — not even a mention of "up to" specifications — which precisely reflects just how badly the PC market has been hammered in the current memory shortage. Even the laptop's main selling point carries a major hidden concern: HP devotes a great deal of space in its announcement to its 2.5K OLED display, but that version will not ship until March 2027. The version going on sale at Best Buy later this month will come with a 2K OLED display, with brightness dropping dramatically from 650 nits to just 300 nits.

Many questions remain unanswered, and some of the answers so far are underwhelming. But if you are still interested in HP's laptop, keep an eye out for more details to be announced before it officially goes on sale.
